title: Water-to-Cement (w/c) Ratio
desc: Determines capillary porosity, compressive strength, and permeability. A 0.38 ratio is required for complete hydration, combining 0.22 for chemical binding and 0.16 for gel water. Practical architectural applications use ratios of 0.45 to 0.65 to ensure formwork workability. Excess water evaporates, leaving an interconnected pore network that reduces thermal conductivity but increases moisture and weathering agent penetration.

title: Hydration
desc: An irreversible, exothermic chemical reaction where cement consumes water to form a solid structural matrix. In massive architectural elements, hydration heat can cause thermal cracking if external cooling outpaces the internal core. The primary reaction dictating early strength is: 2(3CaO * SiO2) + 6H2O -> 3CaO * 2SiO2 * 3H2O + 3Ca(OH)2.

title: Calcium Silicate Hydrate (C-S-H) Gel
desc: The primary structural binder, constituting 50 to 60 percent of hydrated paste volume. It is an amorphous nanoscale gel providing cohesion through ionic bonds and van der Waals forces. Its internal structure dictates water retention, which directly influences macro-scale structural shrinkage and creep over the building's lifespan.

title: Interfacial Transition Zone (ITZ)
desc: A highly porous boundary region, 10 to 50 micrometers wide, located between cement paste and aggregate. Caused by the wall effect, cement particles fail to pack densely against large stones, forming weak, oriented crystals. The ITZ is the structural weak point where microcracks initiate under tensile or bending loads.

title: Carbonation
desc: A chemical degradation process where atmospheric carbon dioxide diffuses through capillary pores and reacts with calcium hydroxide: CO2 + H2O -> H2CO3, H2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> CaCO3 + 2H2O. This reaction drops internal pH below 9.0, destroying the reinforcing steel's passivation layer and causing corrosion and facade spalling.

title: Drying Shrinkage
desc: A time-dependent volume contraction occurring when unbound capillary water evaporates. The resulting capillary tension pulls pore walls inward. In restrained structural elements, this generates tensile stresses that cause cracking, requiring planned expansion and control joints.

title: Creep
desc: Continuous macroscopic deformation under sustained compressive stress. It is caused by the expulsion of bound water from C-S-H gel and the structural realignment of nanoparticles. Creep causes long-span floor sagging but passively dissipates localized stress concentrations to prevent brittle failure.

title: Supplementary Cementitious Materials (SCMs)
desc: Industrial byproducts, including fly ash, slag, and silica fume, that replace Portland cement to lower embodied carbon. They react with calcium hydroxide to produce secondary C-S-H gel. This densifies the pore structure and increases resistance to weathering and chloride penetration.

title: Recycled Concrete Aggregate (RCA)
desc: Crushed demolition concrete comprising original stone and porous attached mortar. It introduces a mechanically weaker double ITZ into the composite. The attached mortar allows for active carbon sequestration via accelerated carbonation prior to mixing.

title: Superplasticizers (PCE)
desc: Chemical admixtures enabling highly fluid, self-consolidating concrete (SCC) without increasing water content. Comb-like polymers separate cement particles via electrostatic repulsion and steric hindrance. This enables complex architectural casting and ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC) formulation.

title: Calcium Hydroxide (CH / Portlandite)
desc: A crystalline hydration byproduct occupying up to 25% of the paste volume. It provides minimal structural strength but maintains an alkaline environment (pH 12.5 to 13.5), preserving the passive oxide layer on reinforcing steel.

title: Alkali-Silica Reaction (ASR)
desc: A swelling reaction between reactive aggregate silica and alkaline cement paste. It produces a hygroscopic gel that absorbs moisture, expands, and causes structural map-cracking across architectural surfaces.

title: Limestone Calcined Clay Cement (LC3)
desc: A low-emission binder replacing up to 50% of clinker with calcined clay and limestone. It matches ordinary Portland cement strength and cuts CO2 emissions by 40%.

title: Capillary Porosity
desc: The void network formed when excess mixing water evaporates. High connectivity increases permeability to water and chlorides, impacting the weathering rate and thermal mass efficiency of the building envelope.

title: Alite (C3S)
desc: A highly reactive clinker phase dictating early strength development from 1 to 28 days. It enables rapid formwork removal in construction scheduling.

title: Belite (C2S)
desc: A slow-reacting clinker phase that generates minimal heat. It drives continuous structural densification and strength gains over months or years.

title: Delayed Ettringite Formation (DEF)
desc: An internal sulfate attack occurring when initial curing temperatures exceed 65°C. Sulfates trapped in the gel crystallize years later upon moisture exposure, expanding and fracturing the concrete matrix.

title: Chloride Ingress
desc: The diffusion of de-icing salts or marine chlorides into pores. Chlorides catalytically puncture the steel reinforcement's oxide layer without lowering global pH, causing rapid, localized pitting corrosion.

title: Geopolymers (Alkali-Activated Materials)
desc: Cement-free binders formed by activating aluminosilicate sources with highly alkaline liquids. They provide high acid and heat resistance for specialized architectural applications.

title: Passive Oxide Layer
desc: A microscopic protective film on reinforcing steel maintained by the cement paste's high pH. Degradation of this layer via carbonation or chlorides initiates structural corrosion.
